1:
The LORD's climactic portrait opens not with description but with a taunt in the form of a fishing question — could Job land leviathan on a hook, or noose down his tongue with a cord? — and the witnesses divide at the threshold over what manner of creature is here defied. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry frames the whole speech as a second proof of Job's weakness and God's power, and inclines, against the more received opinion, to read leviathan as the whale: it is much larger and a nobler animal; the creation of great whales is singled out in Gen. 1:21 as an illustrious proof of the Creator's eternal power; the creature is spoken of as an inhabitant of the sea in v.31, which the crocodile is not; and the great and wide sea is where the psalmist sets his leviathan in Ps. 104:26. He grants that the ingenious Sir Richard Blackmore, with the learned Bochart, takes it for the crocodile so well known in the Nile.

The reformed John Gill lays the options side by side — the whale, most generally received; the crocodile, urged by Bochart; the orca, a great toothed fish of the whale-kind, urged by Hasaeus — and weighs the very name: leviathan compounds than (whale, dragon, or serpent) with levi (conjunction), from the close joining of its scales, so that the word 'bids fairest for the crocodile,' whose scaly coat is knit tight; and the easy transition from behemoth the river-horse to leviathan the crocodile suits Pliny's note of a kindred between them, both creatures of the Nile.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott come down firmly for the crocodile. Clarke notes the Septuagint's 'canst thou draw out the dragon,' followed by the Syriac and Arabic, but holds the description suits no animal but the crocodile or alligator of the Nile — a creature of enormous voracity and strength, its upper jaw armed with forty teeth and its lower with thirty-eight, clothed in a coat of mail that resists a musket-ball. That crocodiles were caught with a baited hook he proves from Herodotus, who tells how a chine of swine was hung on the hook and a live pig made to squeak on the shore, till the crocodile came to the sound, swallowed the bait, and was hauled to land and blinded with mud; the cord about the tongue Clarke matches with Thevenot's account of pit-traps and nooses cast over the jaws. Ellicott finds 'little doubt' the crocodile is meant, and keeps the Authorized reading of the tongue against those who render 'press down his tongue with a cord.' So the chapter opens on its running dispute — whale, crocodile, or the toothed orca — even as all agree on its point, that no man may so much as fish for this beast.
2:
The taunting questions press on from tackle to tethering: could Job ring this beast's nose or bore its jaw as a keeper handles a broken ox? The reformed John Gill takes the 'hook' of the nose to be a rush — a rope twisted of rushes, such as Pliny reports the ancients made — and the image is of leading a captured monster on a cord. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the picture in the East, where oxen and buffaloes are led about by a ring through the nose, and asks whether Job could so domesticate the crocodile; the boring of the jaw with a thorn he reads either of stringing a little fish on a rush by the thorn at its end, or of the ornaments with which horses, mules, and camels were sometimes decked — a mockery of the notion that so fierce a creature could be harnessed or adorned.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet 'canst thou put a rush-ring into his nose, and pierce his cheeks with a hook?' and pause over the very word leviathan, tracing its range through Scripture: in ch. 3:8 it names the celestial dragon that causes eclipses, in Ps. 104:26 the whale, but elsewhere the crocodile — that natural wonder of Egypt which is also called tannin and made an emblem of Pharaoh's might in Ps. 74:13. The Old Testament, they observe, possesses no proper name of its own for the crocodile, borrowing these larger words to describe it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only that the 'hook' may be rendered 'cord of rush,' and the 'thorn' a spike or hook — small philological notes on a picture whose force all the witnesses feel. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, folds the verse into the opening proof that Job could not so much as catch the creature: he had no bait to deceive him, no hook to hold him, no fish-line to draw him from the water, and no thorn to run through his gills on which to carry him home. The whole drift, the witnesses agree, is derision of human mastery: the questions imagine the crocodile handled like a hooked minnow or a ringed ox, precisely to show how absurd the imagination is. What a fisherman does to the small and weak — pierce, string, and lead them — cannot be done to leviathan; and the beast that will not be led on a rush is set at the head of the speech to teach Job how little he can lead the God who made it.
3:
The string of taunting questions turns from the tackle that might catch the beast to the submission it will never offer, imagining leviathan reduced to a suppliant pleading for its life. The reformed John Gill hears the absurdity at once: the creature will make no many supplications to have its pursuer cease, or to be let go when taken, or to be used gently — it is too spirited and stout-hearted to ask a favour, and such begging is beneath it. Where a lesser prey might cringe, this one will not. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is more reticent, owning honestly that 'there are several allusions in these verses to matters of which we know nothing,' and declining to force a sense that the ancient practice no longer yields up to us.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his running proof that Job could not so much as make the leviathan his prisoner: he could not force him to cry for quarter, nor surrender at discretion, for the beast 'knows his own strength too well to make many supplications to thee, and to make a covenant with thee to be thy servant on condition thou wouldst save his life.' The soft words the verse imagines — the flatteries of a captive suing for mercy — are exactly what such a creature is incapable of; it would sooner devour its captor than plead with him.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as one more stroke in the divine irony that runs through the opening of the speech: God pictures the crocodile in the posture of a beaten servant precisely to expose how unthinkable that posture is. And the point, though the witnesses only imply it here, presses beyond the beast to the man. Job had longed to reason with the Almighty, to lay his cause before him and be answered; the LORD answers by setting before him a creature that will not so much as parley with a hunter, and asking, in effect, whether the God who made a beast no man can bring to terms is one whom a man may summon to terms of his own. The supplications leviathan will never make to Job are the mirror of the demands Job can never make of God; and the whole train of unanswerable questions is bending, verse by verse, toward that humbling recognition, that the creature which will not sue to a man is the standing rebuke of a man who would have God sue to him.
4:
If the beast will not beg, still less will it bind itself by treaty, and the fourth question presses the mockery further, into the language of contract and lifelong service. The reformed John Gill reads the covenant Job is invited to strike as one of friendship or servitude — an agreement by which the creature would enter his household and serve him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in 'a servant for ever' a plain echo of the law of the Hebrew bondman, who, loving his master, would have his ear bored through with an awl and so abide in the house for ever, and asks whether Job could so hire and hold the crocodile as one binds a willing slave — an allusion, he suggests, to the statute of Exod. 21:6. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott answers the question with a single dry observation that settles it: the crocodile is 'probably quite untameable,' and no covenant is possible with a beast that cannot be brought to serve.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the verse within the same frame he has drawn over the whole passage, that Job could not make the leviathan his prisoner nor reduce him to service: the creature is too strong and too wild to be bound by any terms a man might offer, and would never enter into covenant to be his perpetual servant. What the verse imagines — a lifelong indenture, the monster domesticated into the yard like a bought slave — is held up only to be laughed away.

The witnesses agree, and again the irony reaches past the animal. Covenant is the very ground on which Job has hoped to meet God: he has wished to set his cause in order and have the Almighty enter, as it were, into a fair agreement of pleadings. The LORD's questions quietly remind him that even a creature of the Nile will make no covenant with man, will take no yoke and wear no collar; and if the crocodile is thus untameable and uncovenantable, how much more is its Maker beyond the reach of any terms a creature might propose. The beast that cannot be hired for a servant is set before Job to teach him whose servant he himself is. The question that opens as a jest about hiring a monster closes as a summons to submission: he who cannot so much as engage the beast in service has no standing to dictate service to its Maker.
5:
From covenant the taunt drops to play, and the incongruity sharpens: could Job make a pet of this monster and hand it to the girls of his house for a plaything? The reformed John Gill catches the grim joke in the word 'play' — the leviathan does indeed sport in the sea, its own element, but there is no playing with him by land, no taking him in hand or cage as one keeps a tame bird. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the domestic picture the Hebrew suggests, that the beast might be tamed into a household pet and given to the little maidens as a toy; he sees behind the phrase the old custom, as execrable as it is ancient, of catching small birds, tying a string to their legs, and giving them to children to torment for amusement — and asks whether so terrible a creature could be so trifled with.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry states the point the verse turns on: there are creatures so little and so weak as to be easily restrained and triumphed over, kept in a cage as a bird for the children to play with; 'but the leviathan is not one of these: he is made to be the terror, not the sport and diversion, of mankind.' That single antithesis — terror, not sport — gathers the whole run of questions to a head. The beast was fashioned to appal, not to amuse; and the imagination of a crocodile leashed for a child's game is meant to collapse under its own absurdity.

The witnesses do not divide, and the movement of the speech is plain in their agreement. Each question — hook, ring, covenant, cage — tries the creature by one of the ways men master lesser things, and each fails; the ascending series measures how wholly the leviathan stands outside the circle of what human hands can catch, bind, hire, or tame. And the maidens who cannot be given a crocodile to play with stand, in the logic of the speech, for every human presumption that would make the untameable serviceable, would take what God has made for terror and reduce it to a plaything. The verse is light in tone and heavy in aim: it teaches, by a child's failed game, the reach of a power no child of man commands; and the crocodile that no maiden may lead on a string is set beside the God whom no man may bend to his own will.
6:
The questions move from the sport of catching to the profit of it, imagining a company of fishermen sitting down to feast on the beast or dividing him for sale in the market. The reformed John Gill reads the 'banquet' as the celebration such partners might hold over a great catch, and finds in the question its own denial: there will be no such feast, because the creature is not to be taken. He notes in passing a mark that bears on the old dispute over the animal's identity — the flesh of crocodiles is said to be eaten and even savoury, whereas the flesh of the whale is not, so that the very question of a banquet fits the one better than the other. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the custom: could Job and his fellows feast on leviathan as on a camel killed for the purpose, or sell his flesh to the buyers as they would an ox? and he cites Herodotus, that at Apollonople and Elephantis in Egypt the people did indeed kill and eat crocodiles.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prefers to render the line of the trade rather than the table — 'shall the bands of fishermen make traffic of him?' — judging that this suits the parallel with the merchants better than the alternative 'dig a pit for him.' The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole question as the failure of men to enrich themselves with the spoil of the beast: 'shall they part him among the merchants,' the bones to one and the oil to another? If they could catch him they would; but, he observes shrewdly, it is probable the art of fishing for whales had not in Job's day been brought to the perfection it has since reached, so that the profit the verse imagines was, for those hearers, no profit at all.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only weighing, as they pass, which creature the details best fit. Together they carry forward the descending scale of the taunt: the beast that could not be caught for sport cannot be carved for gain either, neither served at the feast nor sold at the stall. And beneath the commercial figure lies the same lesson the whole passage presses — that leviathan is no article of human commerce, no quarry to be reckoned in profit and loss, but a creature set beyond the market as beyond the cage, to remind Job that its Maker is not a party to any bargain of ours.
7:
Now the taunt takes up the weapons of the whale-fishery, the barbed iron and the fish-spear, and asks whether Job could drive them home into so armoured a hide. The reformed John Gill weighs the question against the rival identifications. If leviathan be the whale, its skin and body are in fact pierced with harpoons and lances and cut up with knives, so the taunt would lose its edge; the words fit better the crocodile, whose skin is so hard and so closely set with scales as to be impenetrable. He offers, too, the alternative rendering 'wilt thou fill ships with his skin, and the fishermen's boat with his head?' — which again tells against the whale, since ships of many nations are yearly loaded with its skin, flesh, and bones. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse of harpoon-work such as is used on whales, but insists the crocodile's back cannot be so pierced: Herrera, he reports, saw a crocodile defend itself against thirty men and take six musket-balls without a wound, being vulnerable only under the belly.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lift their eyes from the weaponry to the argument it serves, for with this verse they gather the concluding inference of the whole description. If the strength of a single creature of God's hand admits no thought of attacking it, how much more should the greatness of the Creator deter a man from all resistance — 'and who is it who could stand before Me?' No one, they urge, has any claim upon God such that he might come before him with a demand; the terror of the beast is a schoolmaster to teach the terror of its Maker.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the failure of every attempt to destroy the beast: Job could not fill his head with fish-spears, for the creature keeps out of the reach of their instruments of slaughter, or, if they touch him, cannot touch him to the quick. The witnesses do not finally divide over the animal, though Gill and Clarke both let the impenetrable hide argue for the crocodile; they agree that the point of the verse is not zoology but incapacity, and that the barbed iron which glances off the beast is a figure of every human effort to master what God has made — and, past that, of the folly of contending with God himself.
8:
A single imperative interrupts the questions — 'lay thine hand upon him' — and the witnesses hear in it not an invitation but a dare charged with warning, a challenge Job is meant to decline. The reformed John Gill keeps it short and grave: let Job lay his hand on the beast if he can or dares, for it is a perilous thing to do, whether the creature be whale or crocodile. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the older translators to sharpen the menace: Heath renders it 'be sure thou strike home; mind thy blow; rely not upon a second stroke,' and Good, 'make ready thy hand against him; dare the contest; be firm.' The sense, Clarke says, is that of a mortal hazard — be sure of thy advantage, for if thou miss the first blow thou art ruined; kill him at once, or he will kill thee.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the clause 'remember the battle' as a threat wrapped in a memory: 'bear in mind what thou dost attempt, and thou wilt not do it again.' The one encounter is its own deterrent; a man who has felt what it is to strive with such a creature does not return for a second trial. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the whole verse into counsel: Job is told, at his peril, to lay his hand upon the beast — 'touch him if thou dare; remember the battle, how unable thou art to encounter such a force, and what is therefore likely to be the issue, and do no more, but desist from the attempt.' It is good, Henry adds, to remember the battle before we engage in a war, and to put off the harness in time if we foresee the fight is hopeless.

And here Henry alone lifts the admonition to its true object. Job is hereby warned not to proceed in his controversy with God, but to make his peace with him, remembering how that battle must certainly end if it comes to an engagement; better, as the prophet urges, to take hold of God's strength and make peace with him than to set the briers and thorns of our resistance against a devouring fire, as in Isa. 27:4-5. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the hinge on which the beast-description turns from marvel to moral: to lay a hand on leviathan is to court destruction, and the God who made him is a still more dreadful adversary to provoke.
9:
The dare of the previous verse yields to a flat verdict on the hope of ever prevailing: the very expectation of taking leviathan is vain, and the sight of him alone will lay a man low. The reformed John Gill reads 'the hope of him' as the hope of getting the mastery, and grants a careful qualification — crocodiles and whales have in fact been taken, so the taking is not simply impossible; yet the orca, the great toothed whale, has, he says, never been taken and killed, and it is of some such invincible creature that the verse speaks. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the warning to the moment of attack: if a man miss his first advantage there is no hope afterward, for the very sight of this terrible monster would dissipate his courage unless he had a sure retreat or a mortal blow already struck. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the 'hope' as the hope of the rash man who would venture the assault, and the 'sight' as the sight of the infuriated crocodile, before which the boldest is cast down.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states it in a phrase — the hope in view is 'the hope of taking or conquering him' — and leaves the vanity of it to speak for itself. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the several threads together: it is to no purpose to attempt the thing, for so formidable is the beast that if men go about to seize him the very sight of him will appal them and make a stout man ready to faint away — 'shall not one be cast down even at the sight of him?' — and will not that alone deter the pursuers from their design?

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse marks a turn in the speech's logic. The long file of questions has shown that leviathan cannot be caught, bound, hired, tamed, carved, or wounded; now comes the summary sentence that the attempt is hopeless from the first, the hunter overthrown before a blow is struck merely by looking on his prey. That collapse of the beholder is the pivot on which the next verses swing from the creature to the Creator: if no man dares even to face the beast, the question is already forming that the LORD will spring — who then is he that can stand before its Maker?
10:
Here the description gathers to its first great turn, from the beast that none dare rouse to the God whom none can withstand. The reformed John Gill grounds the first clause in the creature's habits: the crocodile lies down and sleeps on the ground, and in the water by night, and it is a dangerous thing to arouse him, so that few have courage to dare it — as whales, too, have been seen lying asleep near shore like rocks, even forty together, no man venturing among them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the point home: the most courageous of men dare not provoke the crocodile to fight nor rouse him at his repose, and the strongest cannot match him — and this is precisely the use to which God turns the whole terrible portrait: 'if thou canst not stand against the crocodile, one of the creatures of my hand, how canst thou resist me, who am his Maker?'

The grammatical-historical voices set the inference in its full weight. Charles Ellicott paraphrases the divine reasoning — 'if the creatures of My hand strike so much terror, how far more terrible must I be? if thou canst not save thyself from them, how much less canst thou be saved without Me?' — and offers, for the first clause, the alternative that the beast 'is not so cruel, even to himself, that he should venture to rouse him up.' Keil and Delitzsch render it 'none is so foolhardy that he dare excite him, and who is it who could stand before Me?' — and read this as the very design of introducing behemoth and leviathan into the speech: if the strength of one creature forbids attack, how much more should the greatness of the Creator deter all resistance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral the verse exists to teach. None is so fierce or so foolhardy that he dares stir up the leviathan, it being known that the beast will be too hard for him; and 'who then is able to stand before God, either to impeach and arraign his proceedings, or to out-face the power of his wrath?' If the creatures put under man's feet keep him thus in awe, how terrible must the majesty of their great Lord be, against whom man has so long been in rebellion. The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the sudden pronoun 'me' the whole point of the chapter break through: the crocodile has been a schoolmaster all along, and the lesson is the unapproachable majesty of the God who made him.
11:
For a moment the description breaks off and the LORD speaks in his own person of his absolute right, and the witnesses treat this verse as the theological centre from which the whole leviathan-portrait hangs. The reformed John Gill reads 'who hath prevented me' as, who has first given me anything that was his own, and so laid me under obligation to repay? The apostle, Gill notes, seems to have this very word in view when he asks 'who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again?' in Rom. 11:35. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the two truths the verse asserts. First, that God is indebted to none of his creatures: let any who pretend a claim make their demand and prove the debt, and they shall be paid in full — but none can be beforehand with God. Second, that he is the rightful Lord and owner of all: 'whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine,' this leviathan included, at his command and disposal. All is his, and we are his, so that we can never make God our debtor; of his own we give him. All is his, so that he needs none of our services and is bettered by none — 'if I were hungry I would not tell thee, for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof,' as the psalm has it in Ps. 50:12.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same note. Adam Clarke: 'who is it that hath laid me under obligation? do I need my creatures? all under the heavens is my property.' John Wesley: who can be beforehand with me in kindnesses, since all things under heaven are mine? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes a structural observation, that this sweeping appeal would come more fittingly at the close of the detailed description than here at its head, before the anatomy of the beast is even begun; but its sense is plain — 'who hath first given to me, that I should repay him?' Keil and Delitzsch attend to a textual nicety, the Ker that would turn the next words into a question, 'as to it, should I be silent about its members?' — a reading some feel the more poetic, before the description resumes.

The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the verse the ground of the entire argument: because God owes nothing and owns everything, no creature can arraign him or put him in its debt, and Job's whole demand to reason with the Almighty as an equal falls to the ground before this single, unanswerable claim of right.
12:
With his right established, the LORD returns to the beast and promises a full anatomy of it — its parts, its power, its shapely frame — and the witnesses note both the design of the survey and a real divergence over how the opening words run. The reformed John Gill takes 'his parts' to be the members of the body, or, as the word may be rendered, 'his bars,' the limbs being like bars of iron for strength. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as God's own preface to the description, and finds in it a lesson about beauty. The leviathan is a creature of monstrous bulk, yet there is in him a comely proportion; in our eyes beauty lies in the small, because we ourselves are small, but in God's eye even the leviathan is comely — and if the Maker pronounce the whale or the crocodile so, it is not for us to call any of the works of his hands ugly or ill-favoured. God here gives us, as it were, an anatomical view of the beast, for his works appear most excellent, and his wisdom and power appear most, when they are taken in pieces and viewed part by part.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, holds that the Authorized rendering is 'most certainly no just translation' of the original. The Vulgate has 'I will not spare him,' and Good would refer the whole to the beast and to God's fearlessness of his own handiwork: 'I cannot be confounded at his limbs and violence, the strength and structure of his frame' — the sense being that the Creator cannot be intimidated by the most formidable of his own works; man may and should tremble, but God cannot. So a genuine difference of reading opens here: whether the verse is God's calm promise not to keep silence about the creature's members and might, as Gill and Henry take it, or his declaration that he is nowise daunted by them, as Clarke and Good would have it.

The witnesses do not fall out over the substance, for both readings serve the one end. Whether God undertakes to display the beast or professes his mastery of it, the purpose of the coming anatomy is the same: to lead Job, part by part and terror by terror, from the shapely dread of the creature to the unshaken majesty of the Maker who fashioned every joint of it and fears no member he has made.
13:
The anatomy begins at the outside, with two images the witnesses labour to render — the 'face of his garment' and the 'double bridle' — both of them, they agree, ways of asking who dare come near enough to handle the creature at all. The reformed John Gill reads 'discover' as 'uncover,' and sets aside Broughton's notion that the sea is the whale's garment; the garment here is either the fold of hide that hangs over the beast's eyes or, better, his very skin — and who would dare strip it off, to flay him alive, or peel away the scaly coat of the crocodile, which is to him a coat of mail he never casts? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the garment is the skin that clothes the whole body, and reads the 'double bridle' of the creature's fast-shut jaws, which have some resemblance to a bridle doubled — noting that the Greeks called the parts of the face reaching to the jaws on either side the 'bridles.'

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the pair sharply — 'who can strip off his outer garment,' that is, his scales, the covering of his skin? and 'who shall come within his double bridle,' the doubling of his jaw? Who, that is, would venture a limb within those jaws? Keil and Delitzsch take the same view of the 'double bridle' as the doubled jaw, and pass on to the scaled shields the next verses describe. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reduces the whole to its blunt point: 'who can rip up the hide of this terrible monster?'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into a picture of a beast too formidable even to approach. Who dares come so near him, while he is alive, as to discover the skin that clothes him like a garment, or to bridle him like a horse and lead him away, or to be within reach of jaws that are like a double bridle? The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the threshold of the anatomy: before a single scale is numbered, the question is whether any hand can be laid near the creature to number it — and the answer, running under all their renderings, is that none can, for the very hide is unassailable and the very jaws forbid approach; and the survey that cannot begin until a hand is laid on the beast begins by proving that no hand can be laid on it at all.
14:
From the shut jaws the description moves to the opened mouth, and the witnesses dwell on the terror of the teeth within it. The reformed John Gill reads 'the doors of his face' as the jaws, which open like a pair of folding doors, and marvels at their span: the crocodile's jaws have a prodigious opening — Peter Martyr tells of one whose jaws gaped seven feet broad, and Leo Africanus affirms he saw some that, when opened, would hold a whole cow; the poet Martial alludes to the same vast gape. And if the whale be meant, the doors of its mouth are of no less extent, as those readily believe who suppose it was the fish that swallowed Jonah. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the plain sense — 'the doors of his face' are 'his jaws, which are most tremendous' — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott the same, glossing the phrase simply as the mouth, and rendering the second clause 'round about his teeth is terror.'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the reader before the opened jaws as before a horse's mouth, but a horse's mouth grown monstrous: he that opens the doors of this face will see the teeth terrible round about, strong and sharp and fitted to devour; 'it would make a man tremble,' Henry says, 'to think of having a leg or an arm between them.' The image is domestic and dreadful at once — the familiar act of looking into a beast's mouth turned into a glimpse of a mouth made to destroy.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse advances the anatomy by a single fearful step. Having asked who could so much as come near the creature's hide or jaws, the description now flings those jaws open and shows what waits behind them: a hedge of teeth, terrible on every side, before which the boldest examiner recoils. The mouth that no man dares open is opened by the Maker's word alone, and the terror of it is set in the survey not to satisfy curiosity but to deepen the awe the whole speech is building — for the God who armed that mouth, and who alone can look into it unafraid, is the God with whom Job had thought to contend. A mouth hedged with teeth on every side is set in the record as a measure of the folly of that thought, and of the mercy that answers it at last not with the teeth of the beast but with the words of the whirlwind.
15:
'His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal' — and the witnesses find in this line one of the surest marks of the creature's identity, together with a small dispute over what the 'pride' names. The reformed John Gill reads it as notoriously true of the crocodile, whose back and tail are covered with scales in a measure impenetrable, as all who have seen the beast agree; whereas the skin of the whale is smooth — its outer skin thin as parchment and easily pulled off by the hand, its under skin, though an inch thick, never stiff. He grants the reports that muddy the case: Nearchus told of a whale fifty cubits long with a scaly hide a cubit thick, and whales were said to have been cast ashore in the Trent with scales on their backs as large and thick as a shilling. And he records a rival reading altogether: Aben Ezra, followed by Hasaeus and by Broughton, refers the verse not to scales but to the teeth of the leviathan, strong as a shield, since the word used carries the sense of shields. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the scales are 'closely compacted together, as things fastened by a seal,' and finds this true of the crocodile but not of the smooth and scaleless whale; Adam Clarke adds only that they are 'impenetrable.'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers scales, seal, and pride into one: the scales are the beast's beauty and strength, and therefore his pride. The crocodile is indeed remarkable for them; if the whale be meant, we must understand by these 'shields' — for so the word runs — the several coats of its skin. What is remarkable, Henry says, is that they stick so close together that the creature is at once kept warm, no air piercing him, and kept safe, no sword piercing him through; for fishes that live in the water are fortified by the same wise Providence that gives clothing as it gives cold.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the animal, though scale after scale the crocodile gains ground; they weigh only whether the 'pride' be the mailed back or the shielded teeth. And the seal that shuts the scales together becomes, in the movement of the speech, another closed door: the creature is sealed against every weapon, as its jaws were barred against every hand, and the God who so sealed it stands the more plainly beyond all assault.
16:
The seal of the scales is now described from within, each plate set so close to the next that not even air can pass between. The reformed John Gill takes this very tightness as an argument against the whale, whose skin is all of a piece and would not be spoken of as parts set near one another; the scales, by contrast, are distinct plates laid edge to edge. He notes that those who make the leviathan a toothed whale refer the words to its teeth, which number some forty or fifty in the lower jaw, met by as many sockets in the upper, so closely fitted that no wind or air comes between them — though he lets the reader weigh how the following clause will strain that reading. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confirms the impenetrability the closeness produces: a musket-ball fired at the beast in any direction, he has already observed, cannot make a passage through such scales.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, taking up the description of the mailed back, pause over a habit of the living creature that the ancients loved to tell. The crocodile delights to sun itself on the land and then turns its open jaws toward the warm beams; and travellers since Herodotus have watched the little birds walk quietly about in that deadly gape, picking worms from the watery jaws while the monster lies still. The detail, offered as they render these verses, sets the armoured stillness of the beast before the eye, the closed ranks of its scales glittering in the sun.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the scales together across these verses, presses their double service — no air can pierce the creature, so that he is kept warm, and no sword can pierce him, so that he is kept safe. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as one more turn of the seal: where the last verse shut the scales with a seal, this one shows the seam so fine that the elements themselves are shut out, and the creature is wrapped in a mail without a chink. The airtight armour is set in the survey to say, in the plainest way the body can, that here is a thing no assault can enter — and behind it, a Maker no accusation can reach. The seam too fine for the air is the emblem of a defence too perfect for the sword, and of a wisdom too whole for the complaint of a man to find a way in.
17:
The description lingers a third verse on the locked scales, insisting now on their inseparability: joined one to another, they cleave so fast that they cannot be parted. The reformed John Gill dwells on the Hebrew, which says literally that each scale is joined 'a man in his brother' — a homely idiom of things fitted so exactly that they seem to embrace. He allows that this might at first seem to favour the notion of the whale's teeth, set in sockets that answer one to another; but the clause 'they cannot be sundered' will by no means agree with teeth, which are separate and drawn apart, and suits only the interlocking plates of a scaled back. The idiom of brotherhood, then, tells for the mailed hide and against the toothed jaw.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect — 'one upon another they are arranged, they hold fast together, inseparably' — the scales not merely touching but overlapping and gripping, a fabric that no force divides. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who reads the three scale-verses as one, presses again the security this knitting gives: the plates stick so close that the creature is fortified at every point, warmed against the cold and warded against the sword, clothed by Providence in armour that is at once his covering and his defence.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very repetition is part of the speech's art. Three times over — sealed, airtight, inseparable — the description returns to the scales, as if to make Job feel by sheer insistence how wholly the beast is closed against him. What cannot be uncovered, entered, or sundered stands for a creature past all mastery; and the mounting emphasis is not idle, for it is bending toward the recognition the whole chapter seeks. If a man cannot so much as prise apart two scales of the crocodile's back, he is in no position to pull apart the counsels of the God who joined them; the inseparable mail is a parable of a wisdom and a power no human hand can take to pieces. The armour that holds fast, brother to brother, holds the argument fast too, closing every seam by which Job had hoped to enter his complaint. What God has joined so fast that no force can part it is a fit likeness of a counsel so ordered that no cavil can unpick it, and the beast whose scales will not yield teaches the man whose case will not stand.
18:
The survey now passes from the body's armour to its strange fires, beginning with the flash of the beast's sneeze and the dawn-light of its eyes. The reformed John Gill explains the first by nature: those who look toward the sun are the more apt to sneeze, and the crocodile, which delights to lie sunning and yawning with its face to the light, sneezes often, so that the spray of its sneezing, caught in the sun's rays, seems to shine. If the whale be meant, it throws floods of water through the vents in its front, and those showers, lit by the sun as in a rainbow, glitter bright. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the shining almost literally: when the creature spurts water from its nostrils the drops form a kind of iris or rainbow, an effect he has seen produced whenever water is forcibly broken into a fine spray. On the eyes he is fuller still. Under the water the crocodile's eyes are dull, but the moment it lifts its head above the surface they sparkle with the greatest vivacity; and for this reason the Egyptians in their hieroglyphics made the crocodile's eyes the emblem of the morning, as Horapollo records — the same figure the Greek poets use when they speak of 'the eyelid of the golden day' in Sophocles and 'the darksome eyelid of the night' in Euripides.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the crocodile sneezes frequently, and that its eyes, dull and dark beneath the water, cast a bright clear light the instant they appear above it — like the morning suddenly breaking after the dark night. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the eyes as 'fiery red and glowing,' and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse under the head of the terror the beast scatters by its very breath and looks: the eyes of the whale are reported to shine in the night like a flame, or, as here, like the eyelids of the morning, and the same is told of the crocodile.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the first of the fire-images that will mount through the next lines, and mark how aptly the creature's waking is figured as a dawn — the dull eye kindling as it breaks the surface, the sunlit spray flashing about its head. It is a beauty that is also a warning: the beast rises like the morning, and what rises with it is dread.
19:
The fire-images now blaze out in full: burning lamps go from the creature's mouth and sparks of fire leap forth, and the witnesses take the words as vivid hyperbole with a natural root and a moral aim. The reformed John Gill owns the expressions to be hyperbolical, yet finds a ground for them: the great gouts of water the whale throws up may in the sun look like lamps and sparks of fire, and the toothed orcae eject a bright oily matter, the spermaceti, that glitters as it flies; Ovid, he adds, says much the same of the wild boar. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans on a shrewd note of Dr. Young: the crocodile, lying long submerged and forced to hold its breath, sends that breath out when it surfaces so hot and so violently that it resembles fire and smoke — and the poets are bold in the same way with tamer creatures, Virgil making his war-horse 'roll fire beneath its nostrils.' Clarke turns this to a caution against thinking Eastern metaphors wildly overdrawn: the figure is nearer the truth than at first appears. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, agrees the words better fit the crocodile, which breathes like the river-horse, with nostrils so large that it seems to breathe a fiery smoke as from a furnace.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lets the hyperbole rise to its true purpose. The breath of the beast is so hot and fiery, from the great natural heat within, that burning lamps and sparks, smoke and flame, are said to issue from its mouth, such as one would think enough to set coals ablaze; and these terrible expressions are used, Henry judges, to intimate the terror of the wrath of God. For fire out of his mouth devours, as in Ps. 18:8; the breath of the Almighty, like a stream of brimstone, kindles Tophet and keeps it burning, as in Isa. 30:33; and the wicked one shall be consumed with the breath of his mouth, as in 2 Thess. 2:8.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the flaming mouth is drawn larger than life, and that the exaggeration is the point: the creature's fiery breath is a picture, in the flesh, of the consuming anger of its Maker. What the crocodile does with its pent breath, God does with his word; and the lamps and sparks that play about the beast are set here to make Job feel, before he ever meets the whirlwind, how dreadful a thing it is to have kindled the wrath of the LORD.
20:
The smoke follows the flame: from the beast's nostrils rises a vapour like the steam of a boiling pot, and the witnesses weigh both the natural fact and a knot in the wording. The reformed John Gill notes the likeness, often remarked, between the crocodile and the river-horse in their manner of breathing, and reports of the former that its nostrils are very large and open and that it seems to breathe out a fiery smoke, as out of a furnace. The image of the seething caldron, then, is not pure invention: a great amphibious creature, surfacing and expelling its hot pent breath into cooler air, might well appear to fume like a pot over the fire.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the last word of the verse, which he finds uncertain — it is the same term that was rendered 'hook' back in v.2 — and, taking it in that sense here, he would read 'as of a seething pot and rushes,' that is, a pot made hot by a fire of rushes beneath it. The picture gains a homely exactness: not merely a caldron boiling, but one driven to the boil by the quick fierce blaze of burning reeds, as if to say the creature's inward heat is stoked and violent.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the smoke with the flame of the surrounding verses as one sustained figure of dreadful heat, the whole meant, on his account, to shadow the terror of the divine wrath — the burning breath, the fuming nostrils, the kindled coals all belonging to a single portrait of a power that consumes. The witnesses do not divide. They take the smoking nostrils as the middle term of the fire-passage, between the sparks that leap from the mouth and the coals the breath will kindle in the verse to come, and they let the caldron do its work upon the imagination. A pot boils because a fire is under it; the beast fumes because a furnace is within it. And the mounting images of heat, smoke, and flame are laid up in the speech, the witnesses agree, not to satisfy a naturalist's curiosity but to press upon Job the sense of a creature all but volcanic in its inward force — and of a Maker before whose kindled anger the stoutest sinner is but stubble. The fuming nostrils are no idle marvel, but a middle stroke in a portrait meant to make Job dread the very fire he had thought to reason with.
21:
The fire-passage reaches its height in a line that fuses breath and flame: the creature's very breath kindles coals, and fire streams from its mouth. The reformed John Gill marks the words plainly as hyperbolical, of a piece with the burning lamps and the smoking nostrils before them, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the phrase 'kindleth coals' is a hyperbolical expression, denoting an extraordinary heat. Neither witness will press the words to a literal furnace; both hear in them the boldness of a poetry straining to convey a heat beyond the ordinary — a breath so hot it seems to blow dead coals to a glow.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the verse in their sequence, keep the same intensity — 'his breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth' — and let it stand as the culmination of the three-verse crescendo of fire before the description turns to the strength of the neck.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reading the whole fiery stretch together, has already named its purpose, and it presses hardest here. These flaming expressions are used, he judges, to intimate the terror of the wrath of God; the breath that kindles coals is the near likeness of that breath of the Almighty which, like a stream of brimstone, sets Tophet alight and will for ever keep it burning. What the beast does in the flesh, the poem means us to feel of its Maker in the Spirit.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse is the last and hottest stroke of a deliberate crescendo — eyes like the dawn, lamps at the mouth, smoke at the nostrils, and now coals kindled by the breath itself — and that the whole rising fire is a figure and not a fact. Its aim is upon Job. He had wished to reason coolly with God as with an equal; the LORD sets before him a creature whose very breath is flame, and asks, in effect, whether a man will lay his hand on such a mouth. And behind the crocodile's fire burns the graver warning of the passage: that the anger of God is a consuming thing, and that the wise man, feeling its heat even in this shadow of it, will not provoke the fire but flee to make his peace. The breath that kindles coals is the last word of the fire-passage, and its warning outlasts the beast, reaching to every heart that would try conclusions with a consuming God.
22:
'In his neck remaineth strength' — the description turns from the fiery head to the body's power, and the second clause of the verse opens a real divergence among the witnesses over what runs before the beast. On the neck they are agreed in substance. The reformed John Gill takes the strength lodged there as a mark that tells against the whale, which is said to have no neck; yet whatever joins head to body may be called a neck, and the shorter it is the stronger, and both Aristotle and Pliny credit the crocodile with a neck it can move and turn its head upon. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders it 'strength hath its dwelling in his neck,' the neck being the seat of strength in most animals, though he grants the crocodile, shaped almost like a lizard, has little neck, so that the head and shoulders must be meant.

It is the second clause that parts the witnesses. The Authorized Version reads 'sorrow is turned into joy before him,' and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps it, taking it that sorrow rejoices, or rides in triumph, before the beast, since he makes terrible work wherever he comes — what is tossing and grief to others is dancing to him. But Clarke will have none of that rendering: the Hebrew, he says, is 'and destruction exulteth before him,' as fine an image as can be conceived, and 'our translation is simply insignificant.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same way — 'before him danceth fear,' or 'pining sorrow exulteth before him' — calling it a marvellous personification of the terror that goes with the creature wherever it goes; and Keil and Delitzsch render 'despair danceth hence before him,' a dissolution of heart that springs up and flees at its approach. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley steers between, making sorrow the beast's companion and harbinger that attends it everywhere, as the poets set anger and fear to walk before the god of war.

So the debate is genuine: does the line say that sorrow is turned to joy for the beast, who delights in the havoc that grieves all else, or that terror and despair dance and flee before him as he comes? The witnesses do not divide over the neck, where strength plainly lodges; they divide over the figure that follows, whether it paints the creature's own dreadful glee or the panic it spreads abroad. Either way the verse marks the beast as a walking terror, strength in his very neck and dismay running before his face — and the God who set that terror on its course stands, once more, immeasurably above it.
23:
From the strong neck the survey passes to the trunk, and finds the flesh itself knit into armour: the flakes of it cleave together, firm and unmoving. The reformed John Gill reads the muscles of the beast as neither flaccid nor flabby but solid and firmly compacted, a body without a soft place. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same in a phrase — the flesh is 'strongly and firmly compacted' — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the point by contrast with other beasts: the very parts that in them hang loose, the dewlaps and pendulous folds, are in this creature drawn tight and set fast, so that where another animal is slack the leviathan is firm. Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the verse in their sequence, agree that even the fleshy flanks cling close and cannot be moved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the picture into a memorable stroke: the flesh is so well knit, the flakes joined so closely and so firmly, that it is hard to pierce him — 'he is as if he were all bone.' And Henry hears in it a quiet answer to an old complaint of Job's own. Job had once lamented that his strength was not the strength of stones, nor his flesh of brass, in ch. 6:12; here is a creature whose flesh is very brass, compacted past all wounding, as though God would set beside the frail and failing man a body that knows no weakness.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse carries the anatomy forward on its single insistent theme. Hide, scales, jaws, and now the very meat of the beast are all closed, firm, and impenetrable; the creature is solid through, armoured not only without but within. And the contrast Henry draws is the heart of it. Job, wasting on his ash-heap, feels his flesh rotting off him like a moth-eaten garment; the leviathan's flesh cannot so much as be moved. The unyielding body is set before the suffering man not to mock his weakness but to teach it — to make him own how slight a thing he is, and how far the power that framed such firmness lies beyond the reach of his complaint. The knit and unmoving flesh of the leviathan is set against the wasting flesh of the man on purpose, that he who feels himself dissolving might measure how little he is fitted to strive with the God who made a body that cannot be stirred.
24:
The description reaches the inmost part and finds it hardest of all: the beast's heart is firm as a stone, hard as the nether millstone. The witnesses agree almost with one voice that the hardness is moral, not merely muscular. The reformed John Gill insists the words are to be understood not of the substance of the heart but of its qualities — the creature is bold, courageous, undaunted, and unmerciful; and this, he says, is true both of whale and crocodile, but of the crocodile especially, which Aelianus reckons among the pitiless. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the 'heart' the same way, as the beast's nature or disposition rather than the physical organ of life, a courage that nothing appals.

On the figure of the millstone the witnesses add a nice touch. The wesleyan-arminian voices note that the nether stone, which must bear the weight of the upper and take all the grinding, was made the harder and stronger of the two: Adam Clarke observes that it is 'required to be harder than that which runs above,' and John Wesley that, being set to bear the burden, it 'ought to be the harder and stronger.' The comparison, then, is not to stone at large but to the toughest stone men knew, chosen for its office because nothing could crush it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the inward and outward together: the beast has spirit equal to his bodily strength, so that though he is bulky he is sprightly and not unwieldy; as his flesh and skin cannot be pierced, so his courage cannot be daunted. The armour of the body is matched by an armour of the heart. The witnesses do not divide. They read the stony heart as the crown of the whole anatomy: the creature is impenetrable to the last, unassailable in body and undismayed in soul, hard at the very centre where lesser beasts are soft with fear. And more than one of them lets the image glance, as the poem means it to, toward men. The hard heart, firm as the nether millstone, is the very picture of the sinner who feels no terror and yields to no stroke; and the God who alone can break such a heart, as he alone can master such a beast, is the God whose majesty the whole description exists to press upon a humbled Job. Body and heart alike proof against every stroke, the beast stands as the last and inmost proof that what God has made unyielding, man cannot move.
25:
When the beast rears up, even the mighty are afraid — so much the witnesses can read plainly; but the clause that follows, 'by reason of breakings they purify themselves,' is among the hardest in the chapter, and here they part. The reformed John Gill keeps to the clear half: the creature raises itself above the surface of the water, so that its huge bulk and terrible jaws and teeth are seen, and the sight dismays the boldest. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the 'breakings' as the great danger and distress the beast brings, the very word used of the soul's distress in Ps. 60:2 and Jonah 2:4; and 'they purify themselves,' he thinks, means that men who ordinarily live in the neglect of God are driven by such terror to cry to him and to seek to purge their consciences of their sins. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same devout way: when the leviathan rears like a moving mountain in the great waters, the mighty are afraid lest he overturn their ships, and by reason of the breakings he makes in the sea they betake themselves to their prayers, confess their sins, and get ready for death — as the seafarers of ch. 3:8 were driven, some to curses and some to prayers.

But the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns the clause the other way: the 'breakings' are the waves the creature makes, and 'they purify themselves' means the mighty are so beside themselves with terror that they take themselves off, withdrawing as men who must dwell apart for uncleanness — a flight, not a repentance. And the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses that the verse has defeated every translator: 'no version, either ancient or modern, appears to have understood this verse, nor is its true sense known.' He sets the guesses side by side — the Septuagint's 'when he turns himself he terrifies all the quadrupeds,' Good's 'they are confounded at the tumult of the sea,' Heath's 'for very terror they fall to the ground,' and Coverdale's blunt 'when he goeth, the mightiest of all are afraid' — and leaves the sense in honest doubt.

So the debate is real and unresolved: whether the terror-struck mighty fall to prayer and self-cleansing, as Wesley and Henry take it, or flee and hide themselves as unclean, as Ellicott reads it, while Clarke owns that no one truly knows. The witnesses do not divide over the fear itself — that the rising of the beast unmans the strongest — only over what the frightened do; and the obscurity is itself a kind of lesson, that a creature can be described past the reach of our understanding, and its Maker far more.
26:
The description turns now to the armory of men and shows every weapon useless against the beast: the sword that reaches him cannot hold, nor spear, nor dart, nor coat of mail. The reformed John Gill reads that the sword either breaks upon the creature or cannot pierce and lodge in him; and since a sword is no fishing-tackle, he thinks the harpoon may be meant — which cannot enter the scaled crocodile, though it does wound the whale, so that this verse and those that follow suit the crocodile best. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it of the assailant's failure: 'as to one approaching him to slay him, his sword cannot stand; it will snap in his hand.' The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees the sword 'cannot endure the stroke but will be broken by it,' for the crocodile's skin no sword, dart, or musket-ball can pierce; and Adam Clarke pauses only to gloss the last weapon, the 'habergeon,' as the hauberk, the Norman armour of linked rings for head, neck, and breast, referring the reader to his note at Neh. 4:16.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads this verse with the three that follow as one catalogue of futile arms: all the instruments of slaughter men use against the beast do him no hurt, and are therefore no terror to him — the sword and spear that wound near at hand, the darts and arrows and sling-stones that wound from afar, all glance away, for nature has armed him at every point. And Henry lifts the picture to a moral: the leviathan that despises the weapons ranged against him is the very image of a hard-hearted sinner, who scorns the terrors of the Almighty and laughs at all the threatenings of his word.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the opening of the weapon-passage, in which the human arsenal is emptied against the creature to no effect, and they let the failure gather its own weight. Every edge that men trust is turned; the sword snaps, the spear glances, the mail is no defence. And the point, as Henry sees, runs past the beast to the presumptuous heart: if no weapon forged can so much as scratch a creature of God's hand, how vain is every armour a man might put on to stand against God himself — and how much wiser to lay down the sword of his controversy and sue for peace.
27:
The creature's contempt for the weapons of men is now stated as a settled disdain: it reckons iron no better than straw, and brass than rotten wood. The reformed John Gill draws out the scorn — a man may as well cast a straw at the beast as a bar of iron, for neither makes any impression on a back steeled with scales that are to him a coat of mail; and he cites Eustathius, that the very sharpest iron is turned and blunted upon him. The two metals men most trusted for edge and armour are, to this hide, as flimsy as chaff and as soft as rotten wood.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, taking up the closing stretch of the description, keep the same note of invincibility and carry it toward the strange under-parts of the beast, whose belly, they render, is set with the sharpest shards, so that it spreads a threshing-sledge upon the mire — the creature not merely proof against iron but itself edged like a harrow. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse within his catalogue of useless arms: iron and brass are to the leviathan as straw and rotten wood, and he laughs at them; and once more Henry hears in that laughter the hard heart of the sinner who makes light of every threatening, defying the terrors of God as the beast defies the spear.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse pushes the weapon-passage to a kind of insolence. It is no longer only that the arms of men fail against the creature, but that the creature holds them in derision, treating the hunter's iron as a child treats a wisp of straw. The mounting language — first the weapons broken, now the metals despised — is meant, the witnesses agree, to leave Job without a single instrument of mastery in his hand. And the lesson presses through the beast to its Maker and to the proud men the poem has in view: if a crocodile can laugh iron and brass to scorn, what shall a man bring against the God who made it? The armoury is empty, the edge is blunted, and the only wisdom left is the one the whole speech is urging — to cease from striving and be still before a power that no weapon touches. The metals that men trust turned to straw and rotten wood are the plainest sign yet that the contest is hopeless, and that the sufferer's wisdom lies not in his arms but in his surrender.
28:
The weapons of distance fare no better than those of the hand: the arrow cannot put the beast to flight, and sling-stones are to him as chaff. The reformed John Gill reads the first clause of the crocodile's proof against archery — its skin, as Peter Martyr and others report, is so hard that it cannot be pierced with arrows, so that the creature neither fears them nor flees before them. Where a lesser quarry would bolt at the first shaft, this one does not so much as stir; the arrow that would drive another beast into flight rebounds from its mail and leaves it unmoved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reading this verse with the weapon-catalogue around it, presses the same point: the darts and arrows and sling-stones that wound at a distance do the leviathan no damage, for nature has armed him at all points against them, and he is no more afraid of the missiles hurled from afar than of the sword that strikes near. The sling that laid a giant low is here a thrower of straws.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse advances the passage by shifting the ground of the contest. Close weapons having failed in the verses before, the poem now empties the quiver too: whatever men can throw or shoot falls as harmless as what they can thrust. And the image of sling-stones 'turned into stubble' is telling — the hard flung stone made soft and light as broken straw the instant it meets the creature's side, its whole force spent to nothing. The mounting series is deliberate, the witnesses agree, and it is bending toward the same humbling end as all the rest. If neither the archer's arrow nor the slinger's stone can move the beast a single pace, then every long-range assault of man upon what God has made is as vain as the hand-to-hand; and Job, who had thought to reach God with the arrows of his argument from the distance of his ash-heap, is being taught by a crocodile's indifference how little his shafts can do. The beast that will not flee the arrow stands for a Maker whom no complaint can drive from his purpose. Neither the shaft that pierces nor the stone that stuns can so much as turn the creature aside; and the man who had aimed his griefs at heaven is taught, by a beast that does not flinch, how little his aim avails against the settled counsel of God.
29:
The catalogue of foiled weapons closes with a note of the creature's positive scorn: darts are to him as stubble, and he laughs outright at the brandished spear. The reformed John Gill, having met darts already, suspects a different weapon is meant here, and follows Ben Gersom in taking the word for an engine that casts stones to batter down walls — but even the siege-engine, he says, is of no avail against the leviathan. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render the word 'clubs,' adding the bludgeon to the heap of useless arms. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke drives home the futility with a traveller's tale of the creature's sheer power: a young crocodile only twelve feet long, which M. Maillet saw, and which had not eaten for thirty-five days with its mouth tied shut, was yet so strong that with a single blow of its tail it overturned a bale of coffee and five or six men with the utmost ease — 'what power, then, must lodge in one twenty feet long, well fed, and in health!'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers this with the verses before it: all the offensive weapons of men, near and far, do the beast no hurt and are no terror to him; he is so hardy that he laughs at the shaking of the spear, as though the very threat of the weapon were a jest.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse seals the weapon-passage on a note of derision. It is not merely that the darts fail, but that the creature mocks them; the brandished spear that would daunt another foe only moves the leviathan to laughter. And Clarke's anecdote gives the laughter its ground — a beast that can toss men and cargo with a flick of its tail while starved and bound has no cause to fear the arms ranged against it. The witnesses let the mockery make its point upon the proud. The leviathan laughing at the spear is the emblem, as Henry has said, of the hard heart that laughs at the threatenings of God; and the poem sets the picture before Job so that he may not be found among the mockers, but may learn, from a creature that fears no weapon, to fear the God whom no creature can withstand. The spear that only makes the leviathan laugh is set at the close of the weapon-passage to empty the last quiver of human resistance, and to leave Job with nothing in his hand but the choice to submit.
30:
The description leaves the failed weapons and looks beneath the beast, where its own body proves as fearsome as any blade: sharp stones are under him, and he spreads pointed things upon the mire. The reformed John Gill reads the first clause of the creature's ease upon what would wound another — sharp stones are under him and give him no pain nor uneasiness, so hard is the hide that meets them. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the same: Adam Clarke says the scales are so impenetrable that splinters of flint are to the beast as the softest reeds, and John Wesley that its skin is so proof against injury that the sharpest stones or shells are as easy to it as the mire itself.

But the grammatical-historical witnesses find a second sense in the verse, that the creature is not merely proof against sharp things but is itself a sharp thing. Charles Ellicott would render the line 'he spreadeth, as it were, a threshing-wain upon the mire,' explaining that the beast not only lies without hurt on the pointed shards but presents a pointed surface of its own to the mud it rests on; its under parts are set with scales like spikes, so that where it lies it prints the ground as a threshing-sledge prints the corn. Keil and Delitzsch render to the same effect, the belly furnished with the sharpest shards, spreading a threshing-sledge upon the slime.

The witnesses do not divide; they only draw out the two edges of the one image. On the one hand the leviathan feels nothing of the sharpness beneath it — the flint is to it as down; on the other, it turns a sharpness of its own against the earth, harrowing the mud where it drags. Both belong to the single portrait the passage has been building, of a creature that neither takes hurt nor gives quarter. And the verse rounds off the long demonstration of invincibility that began with the broken sword: not only can no weapon of man wound the beast, but the very stones that would gall another lie easy under it, and its own body is edged like a harrow. The whole is set before Job, the witnesses agree, to leave him without a single point of vantage against the creature — and so without any standing at all against the God who made it proof, above and below, on every side.
31:
The survey turns from the beast's body to the water it churns, which seethes at its passage like a boiling pot: it makes the deep to boil, and the sea like a pot of ointment. The reformed John Gill reads the boiling of the deep as the violent agitation the creature stirs, the waves tossing and foaming under its motion; and here he thinks the words suit the whale better than the crocodile, whose motion in the water is not so vehement. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes 'the sea like a pot of ointment' of the froth thrown up by the strong agitation of the water near the bottom, rising to the top like the scum of an unguent; though he notes too that the crocodile carries so strong a scent of musk that it imparts the smell to the water it passes through, so that the comparison to a pot of ointment may even be literal.

Two of the witnesses pause over the word 'sea,' lest it settle the creature's identity too quickly. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that 'the sea' need not mean the salt water at all, for the Nile is still called the sea by the Arabs, as many great rivers are — an old usage he likens to the 'sea-wall' of the Thames below Gravesend. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same at length: the great river Nile is called a sea in Scripture, as in Isa. 11:15, and Euphrates the sea of Babylon in Isa. 21:1, and lakes are most often called seas throughout the Bible — and in such rivers and lakes the crocodile has its home no less than in the open water.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the plain force of the image: the beast's very motion troubles the water and puts it into a ferment, raising a great froth and foam upon the surface, such as rises on a boiling pot, especially a pot of boiling ointment. The witnesses do not finally divide, though Gill leans to the whale and the rest keep the Nile and its crocodile in view; they agree that the verse widens the portrait from the creature to its element, showing a beast so mighty that the deep itself boils where it goes. And the boiling sea, like the fiery breath before it, magnifies the terror — a power that unsettles the very waters is set before Job to teach him whose hand it is that stirs the deep, and how little the man can trouble the counsels of a God who troubles the sea for his own ends.
32:
Behind the boiling water the creature leaves a gleaming wake, a shining path that turns the dark deep hoary as with age. The reformed John Gill reads the shining of the path as the white froth raised by the beast's vehement motion, or else the bright oily matter it casts out; and he notes that whales are said to cut and plough the sea so as to leave a glittering track behind them, a shining furrow reaching, by some reports, the length of a German mile. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the path shines with the white froth and foam churned up in the creature's passage, the very thing men may see in the wake of a ship by night.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the shining a further cause from his own observation at sea. In certain states of the weather, he says, a rapid motion through the water disengages many sparks of phosphoric fire; and he tells how once, on a clear night with a good breeze and a fast vessel, he leaned over the stern and watched for hours as the ship's wake became a stream of fire, millions of particles of light struck from the water by the swift motion, as from an electric cylinder, and absorbed again a little way astern. Such a track of living fire the leviathan draws after it through the deep.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the shining path as one of the marvels that set the creature apart: it makes a path to shine after it, which even a ship in the midst of the sea does not, so that one may trace the leviathan under water by the bubbles it leaves upon the surface — and yet who, tracing it so, dares come near? He sets it beside the wonder of Prov. 30:19, the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, that leaves no lasting print. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the last of the water-marvels, the beast's wake glittering white or afire behind it, the deep gone grey as an old man's head in its trail. And the image, for all its beauty, keeps the purpose of the whole: a creature that writes its passage in light upon the sea, and yet cannot be caught by the very track it leaves, is one more proof of a power beyond pursuit — and its Maker, who paves the deep with such splendour, is farther still beyond the reach of the man who would trace and question him.
33:
As the description nears its close, it sets the creature above all its fellows: upon earth there is not his like, a thing made without fear. The reformed John Gill takes the 'likeness' first of form — most sea-creatures have some counterpart on land, the sea-horse or sea-calf answering to their kind, and the crocodile has a sort of likeness in the lizard; but for bulk and terror the leviathan stands alone, with nothing on the earth to match it, as the Targum too confesses. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse of the creature's unrivalled might: there is no animal among the beasts of the earth so thoroughly dangerous, so exceedingly strong, and so hard to wound or slay; and 'made without fear' he takes of a boldness beyond any other creature's — perhaps no beast acquainted with man is so wholly destitute of fear as the crocodile.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his concluding view of the beast as a non-such among the creatures: none in this world is comparable to him for strength and terror. He notes that the earth may here be set off against the sea — the leviathan's dominion is not on the land but in the waters — and reads it as a mercy so ordered: it is well for man that so terrible a creature is confined to the deep, with a watch set upon it by Providence, as in ch. 7:12, for were such a thing let loose to range the dry land, the earth would be no safe or comfortable dwelling for the children of men. And the 'made without fear' Henry takes of its very constitution: the creatures are as they are made, and this one has courage bred in its frame, where others seem as much designed for flight as this for fighting.

The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the summing word of the whole anatomy — the creature peerless on earth, fashioned fearless to the core — and let the two claims stand together, its uniqueness and its dauntlessness. And both point past the beast. A thing that has no like and knows no fear is the nearest the visible creation comes to an image of its Maker's incomparable power; yet it is only an image, a made thing set in the waters and watched, while the God who made it is truly without peer and without dread. The verse lifts the leviathan as high as a creature can go precisely to prepare the last stroke, in which even this king of terrors is owned to have a King above him.
34:
The description ends on its loftiest and most disputed note — the beast that beholds all high things and reigns a king over all the children of pride — and here the witnesses divide both over who is the subject of the sentence and over what, in the end, the leviathan is. On the plain reading the beast itself is meant. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes it so: though lodged in the deep, the creature beholds all high things — the rolling waves, the impending rocks, the ships under sail — with contempt, thinking nothing able to lessen or threaten him; he is himself very proud, and is 'a king over all the children of pride,' the proudest of all proud ones, having (as Mr. Caryl expounds it) more to be proud of than the proudest of men. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds that no animal in the waters does not fear and fly from him, so that the Chaldee renders 'a king over all the offspring of fishes.'

But several of the witnesses read the last clause of God, not the beast. The reformed John Gill takes it so outright: it is God, who made leviathan, that 'beholdeth all high things,' doing what Job was bidden and could not — beholding every one that is proud and abasing him; and therefore Job ought to own his sovereignty and submit. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same way: God can tame both behemoth and leviathan, stout-hearted as they are, and it is he that beholds all high things and is King over all the children of pride, whether brutal or rational, making them bend or break before him. Even Henry grants the reading, that he who beholds all high things is King over the proud, able to tame the behemoth of ch. 40:19 and the leviathan alike — so that the whole discourse proves it is God only who can look upon proud men and abase them, hide them in the dust, and be exalted alone, as in ch. 40:11-13 and Isa. 2:11.

Beneath this runs the older question of what the creature signifies. Clarke lays out the readings without wholly resolving them. Calmet made the 'children of pride' the Egyptians, and the crocodile their king, since it was one of their divinities and the kings of Egypt bore the name of Pharaoh — a crocodile — and the Egyptians were proverbial for the pride rebuked in Ezek. 32:12. Houbigant read the coupled dragon as emblematical of Satan, who lifts his proud look to God and is king over all the sons of pride, the governor of every haughty, impious man. Others take the 'sons of pride' for men simply, whom God confounds by setting before them a creature none can conquer. And Clarke ends in open doubt whether whale or crocodile is meant at all, half inclining to some extinct monster of the waters, and confessing plainly, 'we have yet to learn what leviathan is.'

So the chapter closes on a knot the witnesses do not untie: whether the last word crowns the beast as king of the proud or the God who reigns above the proud, and whether the leviathan is the crocodile of the Nile, the emblem of Egypt, the figure of Satan, or a wonder now lost. What they do not doubt is the aim of it all. The long portrait of a creature past catching, taming, wounding, or matching has been leading, verse by verse, to this: that the God who made a king of terrors is himself the King over every proud thing, and the wise man, beholding it, ceases from his own wisdom and gives the glory to his Maker.
